title: Measurement of ciliary beating and fluid flow in the zebrafish adult telencephalon
protocol: Euthanize adult zebrafish with ice-cold AFW.
Gently transfer one adult zebrafish into ice-cold AFW.
Wait until there is no body or gill movement.
Prepare a petri dish and fill it with prechilled aCSF.
Cut off the head posterior to the operculum, using scissors.
Transfer the head into a petri dish filled with aCSF.
Remove unnecessary organs such as jaws, eyes, and nose under a stereomicroscope.
Cut out jaw parts of the head with a small scissor.
Remove the eyes carefully.
Cut the nose part carefully using a small scissor.
Do not damage the olfactory bulb.
Cut the dorsal skull near the cerebellum or brain stem using a small scissor.
Cautiously remove the dorsal part of the skull by tearing both sides of the dorso-posterior skull using fine forceps.
Carefully remove any bones still connected to the olfactory epithelium and olfactory bulb with the forceps.
Be careful not to scratch the telencephalon, especially the dorsal part where the motile ciliated tela choroida is located.
Remove the ventral parts of the head gently using fine forceps.
Cut optic tracts with a small scissor.
Mount the brain explant on a small petri dish coated with Sylgard using a 10 mL plastic pipette.
Fix the mounted explant firmly with a tungsten pin.
Remove lipid droplets above the pineal gland carefully.
Pull out the pineal gland cautiously using fine forceps.
Be extremely careful when detaching the pineal gland from above the choroid plexus.
Avoid pulling out the choroid plexus together with the pineal gland to ensure fluid flow measurement is possible.
Remove the choroid plexus for imaging of ciliary beating at the telencephalic midline if desired.
Take the dura off from the posterior to anterior part of the telencephalon after removing the choroid plexus.
Split the hemisphere of the telencephalon using forceps or a small scissor.
Mount the midline upside by fixing with a tungsten pin after splitting the hemisphere.
Record ciliary beating by scratching brain areas if there is no direct injury at the surface of the midline.
Mount the dish on the brightfield light transmission microscope.
Exchange to aCSF bubbled with carbogen at room temperature through a perfusion system.
Identify a region of interest using a 40× objective prior to recording.
Deliver oxygenated artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF) to the brain explant through an inlet labeled as “IN” and an outlet labeled as “OUT”.
Exchange to oxygenated aCSF at room temperature for 30 seconds.
Perfuse the sample extensively to maintain health.
Stop perfusion only when an externally applied fluid flow impacts the recording.
Locate the region of interest in the telencephalon.
Record the explant using a 40× water immersion objective.
Set the recording frame rate to approximately 100 Hz for 30 seconds.
Use an upright Olympus microscope equipped with a Manta camera and custom-designed software for recording.
Load the mixture of fluorescent particles into the injection needle.
Mount the loaded injection needle on the needle holder connected with pressure injector.
Cut the needle tip open with fine forceps.
Mix fluorescent particles by pipetting before loading into the needle.
Inject the mixture carefully into the ventricle without penetrating the brain parenchyma.
Ensure that injections are made up to 15 nL in the middle cavity of the most anterior telencephalic area, posterior to the olfactory bulb.
Microinject fluorescent beads into the brain explant using a stereo microscope and microinjector.
Dorsally view the brain explant before and after injection of fluorescent beads.
Oxygenate the brain explant with artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF).
Identify a region of interest using a 10× objective prior to recording.
Analyze data using the TrackMate plugin in ImageJ/Fiji or MATLAB script.
Slowly pull out the needle from the injected site to avoid leakage of CSF and fluorescent particles.
Avoid injecting over 15 nL to prevent enlargement of ventricle size.
Mount the dish on a fluorescent microscope.
Exchange artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF) bubbled with carbogen (95% O2/5% CO2) at room temperature.
Find the region of interest in the telencephalon.
Record the brain explant with a 10× water immersion objective at 50 frames per second for at least one minute.
Record the CSF flow promptly.
Avoid injecting fluorescent particles into the brain parenchyma or an inappropriate volume to ensure recording quality.
Optimize injection and imaging parameters for particle tracking.
Analyze ciliary beating frequency using a MATLAB script.
Alternatively, analyze ciliary beating frequency using an ImageJ/Fiji plugin (FreQ).
Choose one method consistently for data analysis.
Use the same analytical method throughout experiments for consistent results.
Install MATLAB, version 2021a or the latest version.
Install ImageJ/Fiji software along with the FreQ plugin.
Follow detailed steps provided for using MATLAB scripts and ImageJ/Fiji if unfamiliar.
Make sure there are no drifts in x and y axis prior to analysis.
Check manually, frame by frame, that obvious features localize at the same pixel position and do not change shape or rotate across all frames.
Pick 2–3 very obvious features in the image for manual verification.
Download all provided MATLAB scripts into one folder.
Set the Path to this folder in MATLAB by right clicking on the folders and selecting "Add to Path" - “Selected Folders and Subfolders”.
Open the “Master_analysis_CBF” file using MATLAB software.
At step 1 of “Master_analysis_CBF”, enter the value of the frequency of acquisition as “CBF.Fs.”.
Click the “Run Section” button in MATLAB.
Select the raw recording file (.mat format) when prompted by the window "Select Files to Open".
Put the desired analysis time at “CBF.duration”.
Set the starting timepoint of analysis in the software interface.
Skip step 1 if aligned files are already available.
Proceed to step 2 by clicking “Run Section.”
Select aligned or raw files from the “Select Files to Open” window.
Enter frequency of acquisition and duration for analysis when prompted in the “Command Window” for unaligned raw files.
Define variables such as lower cutoff frequency, plotting range, and spatial resolution at step 3.
Use 10 Hz as the lower cutoff frequency if not specified otherwise.
Set plotting frequency range from 10 to 40 Hz based on prior work.
Adjust spatial resolution of microscope (e.g., 0.314 μm/pixel) according to instrument specifications.
Perform the fast Fourier transform by running the “step 4” section.
Save the analysis result as a PNG file and one structure array called CBF.
Prepare the recording file in TIF format for analysis using ImageJ/Fiji with the FreQ plugin.
Start the FreQ plugin to set up parameters for analysis.
Click "Plugin" then "JNH", and select "FreQ".
Choose “multiple images (open multi-task manager)” in the “Process” menu to open recording files.
Enter the exact value of acquisition frequency in the “Recording frequency” field.
Put a number in the “Sliding window to smooth power spectrum” field.
Open the recording file using ImageJ/Fiji program.
Convert the image scale to pixel by clicking “Image” > “Properties” and writing “pixel” at the “Unit of length”.
Set the values of width and height to “1.000” in the properties dialog box.
Click the tabs “Next” after checking that each value is written correctly when opening the TrackMate plugin in ImageJ/Fiji.
Open "TrackMate" plugin by clicking on "Plugins"-"Tracking"-"TrackMate".
Set all values to “1.000” at the “calibration settings”.
Indicate the pixel size of the image in “X” and “Y” of “Crop settings”.
Enter the number of images as “T” in “Crop settings”, which corresponds to timepoints.
Click "Refresh source" if values do not match with recording images.
Start "TrackMate" plugin again after ensuring that step 32 was done correctly, if necessary.
Use the default detector, “LoG detector”, and proceed by clicking “Next”.
Set the “Estimated blob diameter: 10.0” and “Threshold: 50”.
Verify detection of fluorescent particles by clicking “Preview”.
Adjust the values for "Estimated blob diameter" and "Threshold" as needed to correctly detect fluorescent particles, based on imaging conditions and particle characteristics.
Click “Next” after verifying correct detection of fluorescent particles.
Open the “masterfile_PlotParticlesTracks” file using MATLAB software.
Find and add folders containing codes and recordings to Path in MATLAB.
Click “Run Section” at the “step1” of “masterfile_PlotParticleTracks” at the Editor tab.
Put information of spatial resolution at "data.spatres".
Confirm that "data" and "Tracks" files appear in the "Workspace".
Run "step2" to recognize particle traces in image files.
Reorganize recognized traces into a new array "data.track".
Run "step3" to plot some tracks to ensure accuracy.
Identify good tracks based on threshold values inputted by the experimenter.
Set thresholds of "tracklength" and "trackdistance" as needed for imaging settings.
Identify tracks longer than 0.8 s and 22.6 μm in this example.
Run "step5" to plot selected tracks with different colors.
